flagged.evidence: The item asserts for every N>=0 that D_N(3/(4N+2))=-1/sin(3pi/(4N+2))<0. At N=0 this point is 3/2 and D_0(t)=1, while -1/sin(3pi/2)=1, not a negative number. The proof's claim that both denominator angles lie in (0,pi) also fails at N=0.

The function and every partial sum are one-periodic, but the item claims at every noninteger real x that the limit is x-1/2. At x=3/2, its displayed partial-sum formula gives S_N f(3/2)=-sum_{k=1}^N sin(3pi k)/(pi k)=0 for every N, whereas the asserted limit is 1. The correct value must use the fractional part of x.

The proof says that Bonnet's theorem 'therefore gives' ∫_1^B sin(y)g_N(y)dy=g_N(1)∫_1^xi sin(y)dy. The cited dependency thm-second-mean-value-theorem-for-integrals instead states ∫fg=f(a)∫_a^xi g+f(b)∫_xi^b g. Its second endpoint term does not generally vanish here: g_N(B) is nonzero for a general B=(2N+1)pi t. A separate reduction to the sharper form is needed but is not supplied.

The proof defines u_+(t)=f(x+t)-f(x+) and u_-(t)=f(x-t)-f(x-) on [0,delta], then says 'Also u_±(0)=0 by definition.' In fact u_+(0)=f(x)-f(x+) and u_-(0)=f(x)-f(x-), which need not be zero. For the one-periodic BV function f(n)=1 at integers n and f(y)=0 otherwise, at x=0 both one-sided limits are 0 but u_+(0)=u_-(0)=1. Thus the proof cannot apply the cited lemma in step 3.1, whose stated hypothesis requires u(0)=0, without redefining the endpoint values.
